claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 can be prepared by arc melting prior to solidification.
A high-intensity, short-duration electric arc pulse applied immediately after melting can act as an additional ultrarapid quench.
The proposed arc pulse will suppress primary crystalline nucleation.
The proposed arc pulse will increase amorphous retention.
The proposed arc pulse will increase thermal stability during subsequent reheating.
Melt spinning of this alloy provides cooling rates of approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s.
Rapid cooling at approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s yields an amorphous structure in this alloy.
An arc pulse can induce significant undercooling in this alloy under accelerated cooling.
Localized undercooling from the arc pulse minimizes atomic mobility and nucleation sites.
Reduced atomic mobility kinetically traps a disordered amorphous structure and retards primary crystallization.
The arc pulse lowers the effective nucleation rate of non-eutectic crystalline phases.
Suppressing diffusive atomic rearrangement will shift crystallization onset to higher temperatures during reheating.
Slow cooling at approximately 52 K/s produces a complex crystalline microstructure.
Accelerated cooling at approximately 3018 K/s after a short electric arc pulse produces fewer phases than slow cooling.
Both the 52 K/s and 3018 K/s cooling regimes result in extensive primary crystallization and several non-eutectic crystalline phases.
An effective cooling rate of at least approximately 10^5 K/s is the boundary for the expected improvement.
The eutectic crystallization onset is approximately 960 K.
The FCC crystallization or formation onset is approximately 1341 K.
The intervention should yield a higher amorphous fraction than conventional slow or accelerated cooling.
Failure to increase amorphous retention or to delay crystallization onset by more than 50 K relative to conventionally cooled controls would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions appear to require the ultrarapid cooling rate to be maintained during reheating, whereas reheating is a temperature-increasing process. The intended requirement is likely retention of the amorphous state rather than maintenance of a cooling rate.
